title: How to Connect With Anyone
subtitle: A Frontier Psychiatrists Guest Post with My Friend Lila.
body_html:
Lila, of Horizontal with Lila fame, is one of my favorite people. My readers, who have all read more than 1000 episodes of my newsletter, are probably harkening back to articles like “Death is Not a Great Customer Experience.” Or, perhaps, my call out to “The Year I Almost Didn’t Survive.” I was an engineer for the first 6 months of Lila’s epic podcast, and we were co-travelers on Clubhouse back in the day. Most importantly, when one of us is having a hard time—even in the tub-there will be a phone call, and support will be on tap. How do you, dear readers, form this kind of connection in your life? You also spend time with Lila’s work, too.

I have written before, numerous times, about the importance of friends. Lila is another how-to manual for making them.

Without further ado, here is the most recent smash hit from Lila. If you go over to her page, you will see a full-on video on which this transcript is built. Take it away, Lila!

Dear Ones,

It has been a year since my friend Craig died, and I reconnected with the love of my life, Zach. It has been a year and a week since my father’s death. It has been nearly a year since my mother’s death.

I have not yet opened the box(es) with her ashes.

I seem to write in seasons, in eras, in epochs, and I have not written for about four months. I was hibernating, nesting, recentering myself in my yoga practice, considering teaching again. I was going to grief counseling, and trying to heal my tummy, forgetting and remembering to date my sadness, and spending time with my love, loving.

My words are not as accessible now, but they will return. They always have. They always do.

What I have done is prepared and rehearsed and polished my Big Speech, the one that compiles my theories about intimacy so far. The one that shares all the stuff that I have made. The most vulnerable one of all.

My hope is that this synthesis of 20 years of research & reading & interviewing & conversing & workshop-leading & teaching on intimacy will usher in a new era of my career.

In January I gave a truncated version of this speech to a warm crowd of 500 smarty pants at Nerd Nite St. Pete. It was my biggest audience to date, and an absolute delight. The perfect forerunner to giving a keynote speech at Adam’s Connection & Relationships edition of his Lifelong Learners speaker series in February.

If you are in the Tampa Bay area, and you are a nerdy sort, like us, I’m pretty certain that you will enjoy this series. And you have, I believe, at least 6 more opportunities to attend. Go! Learn stuff!

I imagine you are a person who longs to connect. I hope this talk means something to you. I hope it brings more joy, more nourishment, and more intimacy into your life.

The more things get AI, the more I want to human. I want to human with you.

I want to bring this speech, this work, and workshops based on my work to conferences, festivals, and companies near you. If you feel inspired to bring me, please share this with whomsoever you know makes decisions about these sorts of things.

If you have thoughts on my theories, if they move you to action, if they remind you of a story you’d like to tell someone, tell someone. Or feel free to reply to this missive, and tell me. I’m someone too.

Big Love,

Lila

Transcript:

I was a pretty lonely kid, and when I was 7, 8, and 9, my mom was in and out of the hospital with colon cancer. She was treated at Sloan Kettering in New York. I don’t have a lot of memories before the age of 12, which is when my parents got divorced, but I do remember this.

I remember going to the hospital to visit her and being terrified that there was a needle sticking out of this very tender part of her arm, which was of course connected to an IV, which was connected to a pole. She didn’t want me to be afraid, so she called her IV pole Tango and she danced with him. And while well into my 30s, I still cried every time somebody drew my blood, I also grew up to become an Argentine Tango dancer. So coincidence? I don’t think so.

[00:01:00]

I just shared with you what I would call a minor secret. Remember this, we’ll come back to it later.

I don’t think it will come as a surprise to anybody in this room that we are living in the most digitally connected, and yet the loneliest time that has ever been. Digital connection, it has a place, and it can keep us from starving, but it will not make us well fed. I’ll give you a little story about that.

In January 2020, I went to Bali on a two month vacation. I accidentally moved to Bali for a year and a half because in March of 2020, we know, the entire world changed! And I looked across the world at New York and I went, Ah! mass graves in Central Park? I am not going home! And I did not go home for a good long time.

[00:02:00]

I have friends all over the world. I’ve traveled a lot; I’ve made a lot of connections, and I was in contact with a lot of people. I was texting, we had Zoom chats where we watched movies together and I was abjectly lonely in paradise. The only thing that kept me from going a little cuckoo was I would go downstairs into the kitchen where the daughter of the owner of the villa where I was staying and her boyfriend were making tempeh, and we sat there in the kitchen and bemoaned the state of the world together.

This was my lifeline. All the digital connection, I had it all, but it was only that, that in-person human moment sitting at the kitchen table that could sustain me.

[00:03:00]

There is a cure for this crisis of loneliness, and it is intimacy, but only if we can expand our definition of what intimacy is and can be.

We use the word intimacy as synonymous with sex, but intimacy is not sex, and sex is not always intimate, as many of us unfortunately know.

So if intimacy is not sex, what is it?

I’ve been thinking about this for so long and I have a working definition, and it’s truly a working definition. It changed three weeks ago, as I gave this speech for the first time in this iteration. So my working definition, which I’m always open to expanding myself, is:

Intimacy is nourishing connection between humans.

The ‘nourishing’ bit is really important because we know what artificial connection feels like. We know what junk food connection feels like. You gobble it up because you’re desperate to have some, and then you’re like, Ugh, that feels greasy.

[00:04:00]

I feel empty. It doesn’t feel good. It doesn’t fill you up.

I mean nourishing connection between humans in both ways. It is the act of nourishing the connection between the humans, and it is the description of what it feels like to have that kind of connection. You feel seen, you feel inspired, creative... fed.

The other part that I want to draw your attention to that’s really important is the ‘between humans.’

Friends, I know you love your dog. I know you love your bicycle. I myself have a Vespa called Loralei that I treasure, but there is a magic in human-to-human connection that is absolutely irreplaceable. It’s because of the struggle. It’s because it’s really hard to sustain a deep, intimate connection over a long period of time.

[00:05:00]

And what is required for that is repair.

There’s always going to be rupture, always. There’s rupture between humans and there’s rupture outside that affects what is between humans when we resonate with each other. And what is necessary for a long-term connection is our ability to repair.

You know how you get stronger muscularly, right? You go to the gym, you pump some iron, you are actually creating little micro tears in your muscles, and then when you rest, they grow back, and that is what we call getting stronger. It is rupture and repair.

So it has to have components, this nourishing connection between humans. It has to be made up of something. There’s some kind of recipe. I thought about this for a long time. I always knew that it began with Sharing.

[00:06:00]

I have to share something of my special self with you... and I just did, right? At the beginning of this talk, I shared something of my special self with you. So is that intimacy? Are we now all intimate with me?

No, because it, it has to go both ways. It has to be a two-way street. It’s not a one-woman show. It’s not a monologue. I share something of my special self with you. You share something of your special self with me.

Is that it? Is that intimacy. No.

Caring is required. Because if I share something of my special self with you and you don’t care, then it’s certainly not intimacy is it?

So is that it? We share. We care about what each other have shared. Are we intimate now?

I felt like there was something, something missing still, and what I used to call it was permeability, which is of course a $2 word, and nobody could remember it, and so then I changed it to Daring.

[00:07:00]

But what I mean is: you dare to allow yourself to be affected. You dare to allow yourself to be moved to laughter, to tears, to change your mind. It’s so incredibly intimate to change your mind about something based on your interaction with another human being! I have this all the time with my gentleman, and it is difficult and gorgeous.

Sharing plus caring, multiplied by daring equals intimacy.

My wish for you, my true wish, is for you is to be well-nourished. That means sourcing connection from all of the different places that are possible. What are those places? I have seven types of connection to offer you.

[00:08:00]

The first that I’ll share is Friendsome. This is not a real word. I made this up. This is a word now! I love it! Friendsome. You know what I mean! It’s all different kinds of friendships.

And I think of friendship a bit as a planet, so it’s got a core and then rings around it. At your core, you have your ride or die. You have your Three Musketeers friends, maybe your hospital friends. These are the people who would stay up all night with you. These are the people who would help you pack up your mom’s things on the night that she died.

And the next ring out, you have your dear friends. They know every – they got all the tea. They know everything that is going on in your life. You share it all with them.

The next ring out, you have your activity partners, the people you play pickleball with, the people you go to Toastmasters with. Adam and I are in the same Toastmasters group. Christian is here tonight. We are a tight-knit group.

[00:09:00]

And then I don’t wanna discount, all the way at the bottom here you see ‘weak ties.’ During the pandemic, researchers realized the importance of weak ties. Maybe this is your barista who you see every time you go in, they know your order and you have a little chat. That’s important. That is a part of Planet Friendship. This, these are connections born of caring. That’s the, that’s the conduit.

{Friend, that was the pointer. Advancing now.}

Next: Familial. Not just the biological, but also the surrogate and the chosen. Chosen family is incredibly important to me as someone who has not historically been close to my biological family. The people that I have drawn into my web for 10, 20, 25 years are my family.

[00:10:00]

There’s all different kinds of family, and then I will call your attention to what is separated at the bottom. There are more sinister versions of familial connection: cults, gangs. Nobody joins a cult unless they are longing for belonging. That’s why. So while these are dastardly versions that can be extremely harmful, I include them in the Familial category.

Professional. Could be your work wives, your work husbands, your work spouses, but maybe it’s also, you know, teammates, band mates, somebody you have a startup with. Teachers, students, people you volunteer with. This is a connection born of labor.

[00:11:00]

This is one of my absolute favorites. I call it Kindred. What I mean by this is: you’ve been through the shit together, or you’ve been through similar shit separately and came together later. So these are your 12 step groups, your bereavement groups, these are connections born of struggle. You may have been giggling because at the bottom I have included some more triumphant versions of this connection born of struggle, like mountaineering teams & Burning Man camps. Burning Man Camps survive a giant art project in the middle of the desert together. So they definitely qualify as Kindred!

Sensory, connections born of skinship, of skin contact. Dance partners, acrobatic partners, martial artists, wrestlers.

[00:12:00]

I include parents and children because we know – we just heard about the incredible transformation that Michael had holding his baby on his chest. And we know that babies who aren’t sufficiently held develop something that they call “failure to thrive.”

This isn’t just babies. This is us. We’re, we are, we are all this way. We, we need skin contact. We need skinship. My friend’s mother, who’s a psychologist, says, “You need eight hugs a day just to feel normal.” Not even to feel fabulous, just to feel normal! I’m– how– Did anybody get eight hugs today? Yes. Yay. Yay for you. Yay for you. Yay for you. I’m so glad! Most of us, not so much, you know. This is incredibly important, the Sensory connection.

Erotic. Connections born of sexuality, all different types of lovers, including shooting stars that just come once.

[00:13:00]

And Romantic, connections born of passion. Now I’ve included relationships, romantic relationships, but I’ve also included passionate friendships because, have you ever had a romantic friendship? Yes, some of you.

I have a friend called Missa, and we met because I was teaching yoga at the gym where she was working at the front desk. And the first time I walked in I was like, “Ahh!” and she was like,  “Ahhh!!” And I just think she’s so marvelous. She’s so– and it turns out she’s incredibly kind and generous and beautiful and talented, in addition to just being an effervescent personality. I don’t want to be in a, in a romantic relationship with her; I don’t want to have sex with her, but I just feel so Ah! about her.

[00:14:00]

Now, maybe you’re thinking, but I have more than one of these types of connection in my relationships. Of course. Most of them are a kind of cocktail. You’ll have multiple intersecting, layered connections in each given relationship. And I wanted a way that you could visualize that.

So this is a star graph... and you see there’s the 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. So you can, you can plot a relationship on this. One way that you could use this is you could, you could do this with somebody you have a connection with, whatever type of connection. You can sit down separately, and you plot your relationship the way that it is now, and they do the same. And then you plot your relationship the way that you wish it would be, and they do the same. And then you talk about it. It’s very spicy, or it can be very spicy because there might be a gap between what it is and what you wish for it to be.

[00:15:00]

Here’s some examples. Not of the gap, but of the, of the relationship.

This is my friend Julene, and this is a very good example of what our relationship is like. We are very silly together. We’ve been friends for a long time. We used to be in a Tango scene together in Portland, Oregon, so there’s some Kindred in there because some shit goes down in Tango communities and, and there’s some Sensory there because– she’s a, she’s a very, very tall, gorgeous modelesque woman. She is a model. And I am not so tall. And I don’t really lead, but sometimes, I would try, I would try to lead her and it would be sort of like Boris leading Natasha, so, we have a little bit of that Sensory connection and a little bit of that Familial connection for showing up for each other.

[00:16:00] This is my friend Deniz, who was a housemate of mine in New York. Long-term friendship. There was so much stuff, living in an intentional community with four– with thirteen other people really puts you in it. And we went through it, not just the dishes, but kicking people out. One, oh my gosh, one housemate, she ran into the street naked ‘cause she was having a manic episode! In New York City, in Brooklyn! All kinds of stuff. So lots and lots of stuff went down.

He is a sound guy, he’s a sound engineer. He’s done sound for several of my live events. We call each other Villa siblings. He’s my Villa brother; I’m his Villa sister. And then we give each other hugs. So it’s a two on the sensory.

Maybe you heard these types of connection and you thought, well, I don’t know if uh, Familial will really be possible for me because I’m estranged from my family. Or. I, I, um, I’ve got so much stuff around touching people.

[00:17:00]

I don’t know if I’ll, I’ll ever have a good Sensory connection. My ask is for you to hold a small candle of possibility. And I’ll tell you two stories.

The first is: I moved back to St. Pete under duress. I was living in L.A.; I was finally giving it a real go at my dream career in Film and TV. And I got the call that said, “Hey, your mom’s not doing too well. You should probably come here.” And that was the beginning of a descent, a long descent. So I came back because I was the only one, and because I felt obligated, and I came back, I will admit, with not so much grace and with some resentment and some bitterness and some anger and a lot of sadness. But I came back...

[00:18:00]

It took about a year I think, for me to get, to wrap my head around this, to get a grip on it. I had a lot of help from Adam. Adam let me live in his guest room for six months. I had a house to live in, but I wasn’t doing so well. Like I wasn’t drinking water. I wasn’t getting up. I was just kind of like a slug in bed. And after about a year and going to Toastmasters, I started to emerge again, and I went to Floridarama, the funky art gallery in St. Pete. And they had this incredible exhibit up, these giant sculptures that I, I call very mixed media. There’s, there’s like Afghan quilts and there’s phones and there’s gemstones, and there’s all kinds of objects that people keep. It’s about memory. What we keep, what we put away... all mixed together, and I saw that they, they were having the exhibition opening and I thought, I have to go. I have to go and I have to tell this artist how I feel about her work.

[00:19:00]

I went and I ran into a guy I had known in high school, ‘cause I went to Pinellas County Center for the Arts in St. Pete. Hadn’t been back in quite a while... and he turns out to be the love of my life. We had crushes on each other in high school, but he was very, eh, aloof and very, very confident, very charismatic, and I was intimidated by him. And as it turns out, he was quite shy and he never asked me out. Now, I had been told by so many people and, and so many philosophies, so many books, that it was not really possible to have a connection..... that spreads through all of the types, and I have it now. I think that’s remarkable.

[00:20:00]

Annie Lalla, who you saw the quote before, “If you don’t believe something is possible, then you simply cannot ever experience it.”

I held a little candle flame of possibility. It wasn’t even hope because hope kind of felt inaccessible to me, but it, it was possible and it is possible. And it turns out that in my 40s, now I get to have this connection that is not just sexual, romantic, but is also professional. This is my greatest creative collaborator I could ever find. I think we have 10 or more sets of characters that we’ve developed just because we’re spending time with each other and doing silly voices. We’re probably gonna make YouTube videos, just to make it, because the entertainment industry sucks and we should just make stuff ourselves!

[00:21:00]

I wasn’t sure if I could have something like this, but I held that little candle flame of possibility.

The other story I wanna share with you is about Sula..... who was my mother. This is actually in the bathroom at Floridarama. I took her there 10 days– 10 days before she died. Obviously, she’s been my mother my entire life. Familial is all filled out. We have been through so much shit together. So Kindred is all filled out. And then there are times when I would share things with her like I would with a friend, and she was a remarkably intelligent woman who studied social work. She was deeply emotionally intelligent.

[00:22:00]

So I came back, I told you with some, under some duress and with some resentment. There were times I wasn’t even sure that I really loved my mother and I was worried that we might get to the end of her life without me being able to feel that and express it. I was very worried that she was gonna be alone, also. But she was not alone because I was there.

We were in Atlanta. Zach was going to a concert. He was giving me an opportunity to have a two night staycation where I could just relax in a hotel bed and take baths and read things and, just take a break from the maelstrom of caretaking. And the second day that we were there, I got the phone call that said, “You’d better come right away.” And I saw my mom on the video call and she was doing this and she couldn’t speak.

[00:23:00]

So I tried to fly home that night. Zach flew home that night. My flight didn’t fly. And Zach went and stayed up the entire night until my flight got in and I came and relieved him by the bedside and he went to work, no sleep. And I thought, well, this is my husband. This, this is my husband.

I stayed there five days by the bedside, on the couch. I was with her 22 hours a day. The Hospice Crisis Care Team was there with me. So they would say, Go, take a shower. You can go, go take, go get some food. Go take a bike ride. And I was so relieved that they were there, that I felt comfortable enough to take a moment for my nervous system to try and calm myself.

[00:24:00]

When they told me, you know, it’s, it’s time. Go, go in there. She was doing the, the agonal breathing. I lay down next to her and I held her hand in my hand, and I put my other hand on her cheek. By this time, my mother, who had three, four languages, had lost them all and went back to Portuguese, her first language, which I thankfully had learned right after college, and I was able to truthfully say to her:

Eu te amo.

Eu te amo para sempre.

Eu vou me cuidar.

O Zach vai me cuidar.

Vocé fez bem.

Pode ir.

I love you.

I will love you forever.

[00:25:00]

I will take care of myself.

Zach will take care of me.

You did well.

You can go.

This was taken by Zachary ‘cause I asked him, right after she died. We washed and dressed her body. Strew the pedals around...

I wasn’t sure if I would be able to connect with her before she passed, but I was able to, and I’m incredibly grateful that I held a candle of possibility.

So I invite you to hold a candle of possibility for the kind of connection that you long for. It might not look like what you thought it was going to look like.

[00:26:00]

Maybe it looks like chosen family rather than biological family.

Maybe it looks like a dance partner rather than a sex partner, but the connection that you desire is possible and it’s possible for you.

The hardest part, of course, is always beginning. It’s the, it’s the little bud. It’s the... the glass between us is so thin, it really is, but it feels so thick that beginning is hard, and takes a little bit of bravery.

Share

I think also now we are the most rejection-sensitive that we’ve ever been ‘cause we’re not as used to walking up to people in real life, inviting people on a date in real life. So it feels even more high stakes than it used to.

So I would invite you to adopt this cabaceo approach.

[00:27:00]

Are there any Argentine tango dancers in the, in the audience? No. Okay.

So in the olden days in Argentine Tango, you would sit across the room from the people that you might wanna dance with. You needed a way to save face, to ask somebody to dance without taking such a big risk, because it’s a big risk to walk across the room and hold out your hand. And then if they say no, then you kind of have to slink back across to your seat and sit back down and everybody’s seen it. But this way, you don’t have to.

So I would wanna dance with Zach, of course. So I look across the room and I make eye contact with him, for a little bit longer than socially acceptable. And then I look away because you wanna make sure that you’re cabaceo-ing the right person. It’s very easy to, to give the cabaceo to the person next to them.

[00:28:00]

And you don’t wanna do that, right? You wanna make sure you’re inviting the right person to dance. So I look away, and then I look back... and should he want to invite me to dance, he will make a little nod towards the dance floor. And I’ll make a little nod of acceptance. And then he can be fairly certain that if he does make the long walk across the room and extend his arm, that I will stand up and we will dance.

The idea is that you take small risks and you wait. You see how it’s received. Not received? Okay, no problem. Just look away.

Received: you can move on. You can escalate a little bit. Small increments.

Here’s four ways you can do that.

You can start by practicing telling people how you really are. To tell people how you really are, you have to know. So connection with yourself is, of course, primary. You have to figure out how it is you are feeling, and if you’re having trouble with that, I suggest you start at the level of sensation.

[00:29:00]

Notice. Do a body scan. Notice where your, where your breath is. Notice what you’re feeling in your limbs. I feel... I feel a little, a little bubbles in my throat, and I feel a little, a little rumble in my tummy right at this very moment. Lets me know, oh, I’m nervous. So if you say, “How are you,” instead of saying, “I’m fine, I’m good,” I could say, “Oh, I’m a little nervous.” And then we have something to connect over.

I started doing this at Walgreens when, when the cashier would ask me– of course, I’m not gonna tell them the whole story about the day, right? I just, I would just do a little scan and I would be like, oh man. Oh, I’m really tired. 99% of the time, the other person was so tired too, and they were like, Oh my God, me too. I am so tired. And then we had that moment of connection.

[00:30:00]

The most profound moment that I had doing this was I went to Publix while my mom was in Hospice care to get a pub sub. And I was standing in line and the woman said, “How are you?” And I said, “Oh honey, my mom’s dying.” And I could almost see the glass shatter between us. And she went, she walked around from behind the counter, she took off her gloves and she hugged me. And in the embrace, she said, “My mom is sick too, and she’s abroad and they won’t give me time off until four months from now. And I don’t know if I’m gonna get to see her.”

Telling how you really are builds a bridge made of vulnerability.

[00:31:00]

Offering a genuine compliment builds a bridge made of enthusiasm. I love giving compliments and I have a theory about compliments, which is that they don’t belong to me. They belong to the person that I think them about, so I need to return them to their rightful owner.

Daniela walks in. She’s wearing fabulous pants. “Oh my God, what fabulous pants you have!” I mean it; I’m really excited about her pants and her prints. She’s Brazilian too, so of course she’s got the, the flowers and the botanicals.

I would, I would compliment this gentleman on his jaunty hat. What a lovely hat! And the, the curl of his mustache.

I try to compliment people on things that they have chosen, rather than their genetic blessings. You get in less trouble that way.

[00:32:00] You can do what I did at the very beginning. You can share a minor secret.

And you can build a bridge made of curiosity by asking one single question.

Now, listen, I know we all have tons of inappropriate questions that we could ask. I would work up to those by first taking the small risks and increasing the amount of vulnerability that you’re dealing with. But I think that curiosity is a gorgeous way to connect, and I believe that sometimes the difference between you and the connection that you truly desire is one single question.

I’ve been playing question games for 20 years and now, now I’ve made my own. The Game! There are eight categories, one for each of the seven types of connection and a Wild Card category.

The Game in prototype form! / October 2022 / Brooklyn, NY

[00:33:00]

Six of the categories are questions, pure questions, and two of the categories are activities. You can play this game with absolutely anyone.

So you’ve got games like We’re Not Really Strangers or the/and, and they’re wonderful, but they’re trying to maximize their profits. So they’ve got the one for the couples and they’ve got the one for the friends, and they’ve got the one for the first date and the one for the long term relationships.

And this you can play with absolutely anybody by removing categories. So if you’re playing with your family members, you don’t want them to know about your love life, then maybe you take out the Romantic and the Erotic categories. If you’re playing with somebody that you’re not certain you want to run the risk of touching, you can take out the Sensory and the Wild Card categories. So you can play this with anyone, to connect with anyone.

The real secret is that just about everyone wants to connect just as much as you do.

[00:34:00]

The thing is that somebody has to go first. Somebody has to be a little bit brave. Somebody has to initiate the cabaceo.

So if it’s you that wants more connection,

if it’s you that wants to connect with anyone,

be just a little bit brave and go first.

Thank you.

I have written before, numerous times, about the importance of friends . Lila is another how-to manual for making them.

Without further ado, here is the most recent smash hit from Lila. If you go over to her page, you will see a full-on video on which this transcript is built. Take it away, Lila!

Dear Ones,

It has been a year since my friend Craig died, and I reconnected with the love of my life, Zach. It has been a year and a week since my father’s death. It has been nearly a year since my mother’s death.

I have not yet opened the box(es) with her ashes.

I seem to write in seasons, in eras, in epochs, and I have not written for about four months. I was hibernating, nesting, recentering myself in my yoga practice, considering teaching again. I was going to grief counseling, and trying to heal my tummy, forgetting and remembering to date my sadness, and spending time with my love, loving.

My words are not as accessible now, but they will return. They always have. They always do.

What I have done is prepared and rehearsed and polished my Big Speech, the one that compiles my theories about intimacy so far. The one that shares all the stuff that I have made . The most vulnerable one of all.

My hope is that this synthesis of 20 years of research & reading & interviewing & conversing & workshop-leading & teaching on intimacy will usher in a new era of my career.

In January I gave a truncated version of this speech to a warm crowd of 500 smarty pants at Nerd Nite St. Pete. It was my biggest audience to date, and an absolute delight. The perfect forerunner to giving a keynote speech at Adam’s Connection & Relationships edition of his Lifelong Learners speaker series in February.

If you are in the Tampa Bay area, and you are a nerdy sort, like us, I’m pretty certain that you will enjoy this series. And you have, I believe, at least 6 more opportunities to attend. Go! Learn stuff!

I imagine you are a person who longs to connect. I hope this talk means something to you. I hope it brings more joy, more nourishment, and more intimacy into your life.

The more things get AI, the more I want to human. I want to human with you.

I want to bring this speech, this work, and workshops based on my work to conferences, festivals, and companies near you. If you feel inspired to bring me, please share this with whomsoever you know makes decisions about these sorts of things.

If you have thoughts on my theories, if they move you to action, if they remind you of a story you’d like to tell someone, tell someone. Or feel free to reply to this missive, and tell me. I’m someone too.

Big Love,

Lila
